Q: Why is unsigned integer overflow defined behavior but signed integer overflow isn't? A:

Aside from Pascal's good answer (which I'm sure is the main motivation), it is also possible that some processors cause an exception on signed integer overflow, which of course would cause problems if the compiler had to "arrange for another behaviour" (e.g. use extra instructions to check for potential overflow and calculate differently in that case).

It is also worth noting that "undefined behaviour" doesn't mean "doesn't work". It means that the implementation is allowed to do whatever it likes in that situation. This includes doing "the right thing" as well as "calling the police" or "crashing". Most compilers, when possible, will choose "do the right thing", assuming that is relatively easy to define (in this case, it is). However, if you are having overflows in the calculations, it is important to understand what that actually results in, and that the compiler MAY do something other than what you expect (and that this may vary depending on compiler version, optimisation settings, etc).

Q: Debugging Jupyter Notebook in VS Code A:

You get that error because you trying to debug .ipynb file (the file type which works in Jupyter) like a .py (the file type which works in VS Code). So you probably dont have Jupyter extension in VS Code. Download it, then do not press F5 to debug; press the button 'Debug Cell' to debug it

Q: use while with multiple variables in the condition A:

You already got feedback on the issues with your bash code which you could then rewrite as:

$ cat ./tst1.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash

string='Db6laokfKc'
printf '%s\n' "$string"
klen="${#string}"
printf '%d\n' "$klen"  #klen=10
for (( pos=0; pos < 10; pos++ )); do
   char="${string:pos:1}"
   printf '%s' "$char"
done
printf '\n'


$ ./tst1.sh
Db6laokfKc
10
Db6laokfKc

See https://unix.stackexchange.com/questions/65803/why-is-printf-better-than-echo for why I changed echo to printf.

FYI though if you were really going to implement something like this in bash (or any other shell) then you should do it robustly, portably, and efficiently as:

$ cat tst.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash

awk '
    BEGIN {
        string = "Db6laokfKc"
        print string
        klen = length(string)
        print klen      #klen=10
        for ( pos=1; pos <= klen; pos++ ) {
            char = substr(string,pos,1)
            printf "%s", char
        }
        print ""
    }
'


$ ./tst.sh
Db6laokfKc
10
Db6laokfKc

i.e. the bash part would just be to call awk since bash is a tool to manipulate files and processes and sequence calls to other tools while awk is a tool to manipulate text, which is what you're doing in your script.

Q: Surprising behaviour of using static_cast on struct with bit fields A:

As everyone has mentioned, the correct behavior is aggregate initialization, which follows declaration order of members, and default constructs the omiyted ones. So, the expected result with static_cast is .high set to 0xF(truncate the first input to fit in), and .low set to 0(default construct the omitted).

The main problem with your code is that bit fields are not portable. So, std::bit_cast may fail to compile due to size incompatibility, or result in reversed nibbles due to platform specific layout ordering. I would go as far as to considering bit fields not standard layout, but I can't find citations supporting my claim.

If you are going to compile against a specific platform (tool-chain + OS + HW), then the behavior follows the platform-specific documentation. For portability, you should adopt other designs.

Q: can I use dup2() to send output to stdout instead of a Unix Domain Socket? A:

It should work just fine, but it's usually not a meaningful thing to do. The standard 3 file descriptors are often dup targets because they are used by code outside your control (sometimes even from another process). Anything that can take a socket fd can normally take an arbitrary FD in the first place.

Regardless, you will not be able to use any socket-specific APIs, which even includes the common send* family, on a file descriptor not backed by a real socket. The reverse, using the write* family on a socket, does work on all even-remotely-modern systems but obviously does not support the socket-specific features.

Q: What's the most efficient way to implement an array permutation? A:

Okay, this sounds rather complicated but well-detailed. Are there any algorithms you suggest looking into to increase the locality of the permutation? My situation is that at runtime, I need to compute the permutation maps once and then apply them hundreds of thousands of times.

Also, and it is a bit complex to explain, I have a series of N permutations, with some operation carried out in between them:

A <- ... <- C <- B <- A

I think these permutations are not completely determined, in the sense that I can choose different orderings in B, C, .... . From what you say, should I put some effort into trying to find the permutation that minimizes abs(map - [1,2,3,...,len(map)]) , so that, on average, I know I am going to read/write from close elements?
